effects.title: Vitamin C is heat- and water-sensitive
effects.evidence: The vitamin C content of food may be reduced by prolonged storage and by cooking because ascorbic acid is water soluble and is destroyed by heat [ 6 , 8 ].

effects.title: Steaming/microwaving may lessen vitamin C loss
effects.evidence: Steaming or microwaving may lessen cooking losses.

effects.title: Thiamin is lost into discarded cooking water
effects.evidence: Because thiamin dissolves in water, a significant amount of the vitamin is lost when cooking water is thrown out [ 3 ].

effects.title: Heat can raise beta-carotene bioavailability
effects.evidence: Cooking and heat treatment can increase the bioavailability of beta-carotene from foods [ 19 ].

effects.title: Processed carrots/spinach: more beta-carotene absorbed
effects.evidence: Daily consumption of processed carrots and spinach over a 4-wk period produced an increase in plasma beta-carotene concentration that averaged three times that associated with consumption of the same amount of beta-carotene from these vegetables in the raw form (P = 0.09).

effects.title: Cooked tomato products: more lycopene absorbed
effects.evidence: Thus, in humans, the bioavailability of lycopene is greater from tomato paste than from fresh tomatoes.

effects.title: Boiling lowers oxalate (which binds calcium)
effects.evidence: Boiling markedly reduced soluble oxalate content by 30-87% and was more effective than steaming (5-53%) and baking (used only for potatoes, no oxalate loss).

effects.title: Oxalate lowers calcium absorption
effects.evidence: Certain compounds in plants (e.g., oxalic acid, phytic acid) can decrease calcium absorption by forming indigestible salts with calcium [ 3 ].

effects.title: Soaking, sprouting, fermenting reduce phytate
effects.evidence: These include genetic improvement as well as several pre-treatment methods such as fermentation, soaking, germination and enzymatic treatment of grains with phytase enzyme.

effects.title: Phytate binds zinc
effects.evidence: Phytates, the storage form of phosphorus in plants, bind some minerals such as zinc in the intestine and form an insoluble complex that inhibits zinc absorption [ 1-3 , 8 ].

effects.title: Phytate reduces nonheme iron absorption
effects.evidence: In addition to ascorbic acid, meat, poultry, and seafood can enhance nonheme iron absorption, whereas phytate (which is present in grains and beans) and certain polyphenols in some nonanimal foods (e.g., cereals, legumes) have the opposite effect [ 4 ].

effects.title: Raw/undercooked kidney beans: phytohaemagglutinin
effects.evidence: If you eat them raw or under‐cooked, they can cause you to have extreme nausea, severe vomiting, and diarrhea.

effects.title: Don’t use slow cookers for kidney beans
effects.evidence: Slow cookers don’t get hot enough to destroy the toxin in kidney beans.

effects.title: Raw sprouts can carry bacteria
effects.evidence: Furthermore, like any fresh produce that is consumed raw or lightly cooked, sprouts (such as alfalfa or mung bean) that are served raw or lightly cooked may contain bacteria that can cause foodborne illness.

effects.title: Raw eggs: Salmonella
effects.evidence: Fresh eggs, even those with clean, uncracked shells, may contain bacteria called Salmonella that can cause foodborne illness, often called “food poisoning.

effects.title: Egg dishes: cook to 160 °F
effects.evidence: Casseroles and other dishes containing eggs should be cooked to 160° F.

effects.title: Raw milk outbreaks
effects.evidence: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), from 1998 through 2018, there were 202 outbreaks linked to drinking raw milk These outbreaks caused 2,645 illnesses and 228 hospitalizations.

effects.title: Raw milk and pregnancy (Listeria)
effects.evidence: The Dangers of Listeria and Pregnancy Pregnant women run a serious risk of becoming ill from the germ Listeria , which is often found in raw milk and can cause miscarriage, or illness, or death of the newborn baby.

effects.title: Acrylamide forms in high-heat cooking of starchy foods
effects.evidence: Food storage and preparation methods Comparing frying, roasting, and baking potatoes, frying causes the highest acrylamide formation.

effects.title: Soaking potato slices reduces acrylamide
effects.evidence: Soaking raw potato slices in water for 15-30 minutes before frying or roasting helps reduce acrylamide formation during cooking.

effects.title: Acrylamide: animal studies at very high doses
effects.evidence: Acrylamide caused cancer in animals in studies where animals were exposed to acrylamide at very high doses.

effects.title: Cook to a safe internal temperature
effects.evidence: Safe minimum internal temperature — Beef, Pork, Veal, and Lamb (chops, roasts, steaks): 145 o F with a 3 minute rest time.

effects.title: Cook to a safe internal temperature
effects.evidence: Safe minimum internal temperature — Ground Meat: 160 o F.

effects.title: Cook to a safe internal temperature
effects.evidence: Safe minimum internal temperature — Poultry (ground, parts, whole, and stuffing): 165 o F.

effects.title: Cook to a safe internal temperature
effects.evidence: Safe minimum internal temperature — Fin Fish: 145 o F or flesh is opaque & separates easily with fork.

effects.title: Cook to a safe internal temperature
effects.evidence: Safe minimum internal temperature — Clams, Oysters, and Mussels: Shells open during cooking.
